aV7uG4D4-PM.title: See Every Job Your App Has Queued: Action Queue

paragraphs.heading: The quiet worry
paragraphs.text: You have turned on a few automations over the weeks. Do you actually remember what is still set to run?

paragraphs.heading: One list for all of it
paragraphs.text: Action Queue is that answer. Every scheduled job, from every butler, gathered into one place.

paragraphs.heading: Nothing runs from here
paragraphs.text: Worth saying up front. This screen does not start anything. It shows you what other tools have already armed.

paragraphs.heading: The headline
paragraphs.text: This line tells you how many jobs you are looking at, and how many exist in total once filters are off.

paragraphs.heading: The three numbers that matter
paragraphs.text: These are the ones to read first. Overdue, due in the next hour, and due some time today.

paragraphs.heading: Overdue is the one to fix
paragraphs.text: Overdue does not mean broken. It usually means the app was closed when something was meant to fire.

paragraphs.heading: Which butler is busiest
paragraphs.text: These badges break the same list down by workspace, so you can see who is doing all the work.

paragraphs.heading: Narrow it to one tool
paragraphs.text: Pick a workspace here and everything else drops away. Useful when you only care about one butler.

paragraphs.heading: Or just search
paragraphs.text: And this searches across all of it. Brand, keyword, message, type. It filters as you type.

paragraphs.heading: Reading a card
paragraphs.text: Each card is one job. What it is, which butler owns it, and when it is due to go.

paragraphs.heading: The time label
paragraphs.text: This part is the schedule. Overdue, or scheduled, with the real time beside it.

paragraphs.heading: Cards are not clickable
paragraphs.text: One thing that catches people. The cards look like you can open them. You cannot. There is nothing behind them.

paragraphs.heading: The one button that does something
paragraphs.text: This little x is the only control here with teeth. It removes the job from the queue.

paragraphs.heading: It does not ask
paragraphs.text: And it does not ask you first. No confirmation, no undo. One click and the card is gone.

paragraphs.heading: Sometimes it does not stick
paragraphs.text: Here is the part worth knowing. For recurring jobs, the card vanishes but the schedule underneath keeps running.

paragraphs.heading: So turn it off at the source
paragraphs.text: If you genuinely want a recurring job stopped, go and switch it off in the butler that owns it.

paragraphs.heading: What has already happened
paragraphs.text: Underneath, the completed list. Empty here, which is normal if nothing has fired since you opened the app.

paragraphs.heading: The live log
paragraphs.text: And this opens the running commentary. Everything the background jobs are saying, as they say it.

paragraphs.heading: Filter the noise
paragraphs.text: You can cut it down to just warnings or just errors, which is the fastest way to find what went wrong.

paragraphs.heading: Clear only clears the view
paragraphs.text: And Clear here only tidies what you are looking at. The real log files on disk are untouched.

paragraphs.heading: So, the habit
paragraphs.text: Open this once a week. Read the overdue number. If something is queued that you forgot about, that is the point of the screen.

O7MFp8d--YE.title: Pick Your Keywords for the Year: Keywords and Filters

paragraphs.heading: What this screen decides
paragraphs.text: Every brand the app messages for you starts here. This is the list of things you want to be sent.

paragraphs.heading: Add what you want
paragraphs.text: Type a product type or a brand name and press Add. Each one becomes a little tag underneath.

paragraphs.heading: Tags you can rearrange
paragraphs.text: Click a tag to pause it without losing it. Drag them around to say which matter most.

paragraphs.heading: Now what to avoid
paragraphs.text: This one is the opposite. Any campaign with these words in its title gets skipped.

paragraphs.heading: Words that waste your time
paragraphs.text: Good ones to put here are things you would never film. Think supplements, or vape, or anything off limits for you.

paragraphs.heading: And brands to never message
paragraphs.text: Same idea for brands. A competitor, or somebody you already work with directly. They never get contacted.

paragraphs.heading: A missing button
paragraphs.text: Small thing. Only the first list has a delete all button. For these two you remove tags one at a time.

paragraphs.heading: Now the clever half
paragraphs.text: Underneath is a helper that writes a year of keywords for you, one list per month, using your OpenAI key.

paragraphs.heading: This box is required
paragraphs.text: Only one box is required. What do you sell? Kitchen, garden, baby, whatever it is. Nothing runs without it.

paragraphs.heading: Who buys from you
paragraphs.text: Who you are talking to is optional, but it helps. Busy parents get different ideas than student flats.

paragraphs.heading: This is not a hint
paragraphs.text: Now read this carefully. The screen calls these a price hint. They are not. They really do throw ideas away.

paragraphs.heading: It starts at thirty
paragraphs.text: And it comes set to thirty. So out of the box, cheaper products are dropped before you ever see them.

paragraphs.heading: Nudge the ideas
paragraphs.text: These tick boxes steer the suggestions. Things that trend, things people buy several of, things that fix a problem.

paragraphs.heading: Tick this before you run
paragraphs.text: This one matters more than it looks. Leave it off and every run wipes what is already in your months.

paragraphs.heading: Then press this
paragraphs.text: Then this button writes all twelve months. It costs a few pennies of your own OpenAI credit each time.

paragraphs.heading: Watch the months tick over
paragraphs.text: A little window shows each month finishing. Ignore the counter at the top, it stays on zero the whole time.

paragraphs.heading: Here is what you get
paragraphs.text: And this is the payoff. Twelve boxes, one per month, each full of things worth chasing at that time of year.

paragraphs.heading: Edit anything you like
paragraphs.text: These are just text boxes. Delete what does not fit you, and type in anything the helper missed.

paragraphs.heading: Then send it across
paragraphs.text: When a month looks right, send it to Message Brands. That is the list your outreach actually works from.

paragraphs.heading: It goes anyway
paragraphs.text: Although here is a surprise. If your main list is empty, this month gets used even if you never press send.

paragraphs.heading: The one to avoid
paragraphs.text: Last thing, and the important one. This copies settings from another butler and wipes all twelve months.

paragraphs.heading: No question, no undo
paragraphs.text: It does not ask first, and it works even when the rest of this box looks greyed out. Give it a wide berth.

paragraphs.heading: So, the short version
paragraphs.text: Add what you want, add what you never want, set your price floor low, then let it write your year.

zmV9IkoUfPg.title: Automate Amazon Creator Connections Brand Outreach

paragraphs.heading: The problem
paragraphs.text: You already know which brands your videos sell for. Turning that into an actual campaign means opening Creator Connections and typing the same pitch, brand after brand, until you give up.

paragraphs.heading: What Message Brands does
paragraphs.text: Message Brands reads the brands behind the products you have already sold, then sends each one a Creator Connections message for you. You write it once. The butler does the rest.

paragraphs.heading: Filters decide who gets contacted
paragraphs.text: Before anything else, Keywords and Filters. This is the child workspace right under Message Brands, and it is what decides who gets contacted. Leave it empty and nothing is narrowing the run.

paragraphs.heading: Add a keyword to target
paragraphs.text: Add the keywords or brand names you want to go after. Every campaign that matches one of these becomes a target for the run.

paragraphs.heading: And what to leave alone
paragraphs.text: Two skip lists sit under it. Skip keywords in campaign title drops anything you never want to be associated with, and brands to skip takes specific brands out entirely. Both beat the include list, so a skip always wins.

paragraphs.heading: Back to Message Brands
paragraphs.text: With filters set, head back to Message Brands. Everything from here is about what the message says and how fast it goes out.

paragraphs.heading: Then write your message
paragraphs.text: With your filters set, come back here and write the default message. Use brandName and campaignName in curly braces and each brand gets its own name filled in, so it never reads like a blast.

paragraphs.heading: Line breaks split messages
paragraphs.text: One thing worth knowing. Every line break you type goes out as its own separate message, because Amazon collapses line breaks inside a single one. Short punchy lines land better anyway.

paragraphs.heading: Never message twice
paragraphs.text: This stays on unless you have a reason. It skips any brand that already has a message or a conversation, whether the butler sent it or you did yourself.

paragraphs.heading: Set your pace
paragraphs.text: Daily message cap and pause between sends are your pacing controls. Start conservative for the first run so you can read what actually landed in your Creator Connections inbox before you open it up.

paragraphs.heading: Filter out weak campaigns
paragraphs.text: Campaign value filters are where this gets good. Turn them on and a brand only gets messaged if its campaign clears the bars you set for product price and Creator Connections commission.

paragraphs.heading: Stop samples for dead listings
paragraphs.text: These two are the ones that save you from a closet of samples for products nobody buys. Minimum reviews, because Amazon does not publish sales counts and review volume is the closest public signal. Even ten clears out the never sold tail.

paragraphs.heading: Only ranked products
paragraphs.text: And this one. Amazon only ranks products that actually sell, so requiring a Best Sellers Rank quietly drops the rest. Both checks read from the Creators API, so connect it first or they get skipped.

paragraphs.heading: Add a follow-up
paragraphs.text: Most brands do not answer the first message. Enable follow-ups, choose how long to wait, and write a shorter nudge. Variants let it rotate the wording so every follow-up is not identical.

paragraphs.heading: Now press Run
paragraphs.text: That is everything configured. Press Run and the butler opens Chrome, works through the campaigns your filters matched, and posts your message on each brand's Creator Connections page.

paragraphs.heading: Watch it work
paragraphs.text: Watch the run status fill in. Current brand tells you who it is on right now, search term shows which of your keywords surfaced them, and reason explains anything it decided to skip. Tick watch it run and the browser comes on screen so you can see every step it takes.

paragraphs.heading: Follow it into Messenger
paragraphs.text: Now the part that pays off later. Open Messenger Butler. One thing first: run initial harvest once, or this panel reads last synced never and stays empty even though the conversations exist on Amazon.

paragraphs.heading: Search by brand or keyword
paragraphs.text: Once it is synced, every conversation carries the keyword it went out under, and this search filters by brand or keyword. Type a keyword and you see exactly which search terms produced replies, so you can stop spending sends on the ones that never do.

paragraphs.heading: Where to start
paragraphs.text: So the whole loop is: set your keywords, write the message, run a small batch, then come back to Messenger Butler in a few days and read which keywords earned replies. Start with one keyword and a daily cap you are comfortable with.

RdM4F9NyB7c.title: Set Up Your API Keys in Influencer Butler

paragraphs.heading: Why a tool says it is not set up
paragraphs.text: You open a butler, press the button, and it tells you something is not connected. Nine times out of ten, the fix is on this one screen.

paragraphs.heading: What this screen is
paragraphs.text: API Integrations is where you paste the keys that let the app talk to Amazon, to OpenAI, and to your link services. Set them once and you are done.

paragraphs.heading: Your keys are blurred here
paragraphs.text: One note before we start. Every key on my screen is blurred out for this video. Yours will show as dots. Treat them like a password, because that is what they are.

paragraphs.heading: There is no Save button
paragraphs.text: Something to know right away. There is no Save button on this page. It saves as you type, about half a second after you stop. If you paste a key and close the app, it is already saved.

paragraphs.heading: Start with the Creators API
paragraphs.text: Start at the top with the Creators API. This is the Amazon one, and it is the key that most of the app leans on. It is free to get.

paragraphs.heading: Amazon shows you where
paragraphs.text: You need two things from Amazon, a Credential ID and a Credential Secret. Show Me Where opens Amazon on the right page for you. I am not clicking it, because it would put my real keys on screen.

paragraphs.heading: The box people get wrong
paragraphs.text: Now the box that trips up nearly everyone. Partner Tag is your Associates tracking ID. It looks like your name, dash, twenty. It is not your storefront ID. Put the wrong one in and the test still passes, then real runs fail.

paragraphs.heading: Selling in other countries?
paragraphs.text: Amazon gives you separate keys for each part of the world. The boxes at the top are for the US and Canada. Open this section for Europe and Asia.

paragraphs.heading: Then test it
paragraphs.text: Every card has a Test Connection button. Press it and the line underneath turns green when it works, or red with a reason when it does not.

paragraphs.heading: Green is not always the truth
paragraphs.text: Be a little careful with green though. If a test quietly fails when the app starts up, the old green result stays on screen. Press the button yourself to see what is really going on.

paragraphs.heading: The OpenAI key
paragraphs.text: Next one down that matters. OpenAI is the key behind anything the app writes or listens to. Scripts, captions, comments, image ideas.

paragraphs.heading: This one you pay for
paragraphs.text: This one is not free. It bills to your own OpenAI account, by the amount you use. It is cents at a time, not a subscription, but it is real money.

paragraphs.heading: Watch what you are spending
paragraphs.text: This block keeps a running count of what the app has spent. It is the app's own estimate, not your bill, so check OpenAI for the real number.

paragraphs.heading: The cap is not a cap
paragraphs.text: And read this one carefully. The spend cap does not stop anything. It only warns you. The app will keep making calls past the number you put in.

paragraphs.heading: Where your links come from
paragraphs.text: Further down is link routing. This one setting decides how every link in the whole app gets built. There is no per tool override.

paragraphs.heading: Connecting is only half of it
paragraphs.text: Here is the trap that has cost people weeks. Connecting a link service does nothing on its own. You also have to pick it here. Otherwise it sits there connected and unused.

paragraphs.heading: Two that say connected but are not tested
paragraphs.text: Two more to know about. The image ones, Fal and Ideogram, only check that your key is the right shape. They never actually ask the provider. So green here just means it looks like a key.

paragraphs.heading: Coming soon means not yet
paragraphs.text: A couple of cards have boxes you can see but not fill in. Those say Coming Soon. Nothing to do there yet.

paragraphs.heading: Check them all at once
paragraphs.text: When you are done, press Run saved tests. It goes through every card you have filled in and tells you which ones answer.

paragraphs.heading: Where to start
paragraphs.text: So, shortest path. Do the Creators API first, and double check the Partner Tag. Add OpenAI if you want the writing tools. Everything else can wait until a butler asks for it.

Zh1otu8BaGE.title: Turn One Keyword Into A Published List: Benable Butler

paragraphs.heading: What Benable is
paragraphs.text: Benable is a site where people share lists of things they recommend. Your links, your picks, one page.

paragraphs.heading: Building one by hand is slow
paragraphs.text: Finding twenty products, writing twenty descriptions, pasting twenty links. That is an evening gone.

paragraphs.heading: So this does it
paragraphs.text: You give it a niche. It plans the list, searches Amazon, writes the descriptions, and can publish the whole thing.

paragraphs.heading: It is in beta
paragraphs.text: Worth saying. This one is still being built, so expect it to change.

paragraphs.heading: Nothing is running
paragraphs.text: This tells you what it is doing. Idle now, which is where you want to start from.

paragraphs.heading: The one word that matters
paragraphs.text: This is the whole input. A niche. Dog toys. Small kitchen. Camping with kids.

paragraphs.heading: Which Amazon
paragraphs.text: Then which marketplace to search, because the prices and the links differ by country.

paragraphs.heading: Who you are on Benable
paragraphs.text: And your Benable handle, so it knows which account to publish under.

paragraphs.heading: Start with this one
paragraphs.text: Now the buttons. Dry run does all the thinking and none of the publishing. Nothing reaches Benable.

paragraphs.heading: Then this one
paragraphs.text: Preview does the same, and writes you a page you can open and read before you commit to anything.

paragraphs.heading: And this one is real
paragraphs.text: Publish is the live one. It opens a browser, signs into your account, and creates the lists for real.

paragraphs.heading: It does not ask
paragraphs.text: There is no are you sure. One click and it goes. And there is no unpublish button anywhere in here.

paragraphs.heading: Stop while it works
paragraphs.text: Stop is there if you change your mind mid run. It only lights up once something is going.

paragraphs.heading: The settings worth opening
paragraphs.text: Most of the knobs are hidden in here. Open it before your first real run.

paragraphs.heading: The one to check
paragraphs.text: This one. Make lists public is ticked out of the box, so a publish puts them straight in front of people.

paragraphs.heading: Hide the browser
paragraphs.text: And this hides the Chrome window during a publish, if you would rather not watch it work.

paragraphs.heading: Keep the first run small
paragraphs.text: These caps stop it building forty lists on your first go. Small numbers first.

paragraphs.heading: Only decent products
paragraphs.text: And these two skip anything poorly rated or barely reviewed, which saves you curating by hand.

paragraphs.heading: Hand picking instead
paragraphs.text: There is a second way in. Send products from Storefront Butler and they land in this queue.

paragraphs.heading: Say where each goes
paragraphs.text: Then set which list each one belongs in, and publish just those.

paragraphs.heading: On a clock
paragraphs.text: Finally, it can run itself. Pick how often, and what it should do each time it fires.

paragraphs.heading: Choose refresh, not publish
paragraphs.text: My advice. If you do turn this on, set it to refresh. Publishing on a timer is a lot of trust.

paragraphs.heading: So, the order
paragraphs.text: Dry run first. Then preview and actually read it. Then publish once, with small caps, and go look at the result.

EFQco5UQ_qI.title: Comments Written For You: Benable Comment Butler

paragraphs.heading: A like is quiet
paragraphs.text: A like is polite. A comment is a conversation. It is the difference between being seen and being remembered.

paragraphs.heading: But comments take thought
paragraphs.text: Which is the problem. A generic nice list helps nobody. A good comment needs you to actually look at the product.

paragraphs.heading: So it looks at the product
paragraphs.text: This reads the Amazon product behind each item and writes something specific about that thing.

paragraphs.heading: It starts safe
paragraphs.text: And the best bit. Out of the box it is in dry run, so it writes the comments and posts none of them.

paragraphs.heading: Where to look
paragraphs.text: Start with the profiles. Paste in the creators whose lists you want to comment on.

paragraphs.heading: Borrow your like list
paragraphs.text: If you already set up the Like Butler, this pulls the same profiles across so you are not typing twice.

paragraphs.heading: Or let it browse
paragraphs.text: You can also let it work through Benable's own Discover feed, by category.

paragraphs.heading: Pick your corners
paragraphs.text: Only the categories you tick get visited. Trending is on to start with.

paragraphs.heading: Amazon items only
paragraphs.text: This one matters for quality. Amazon linked products only, because those are the ones it can read details for.

paragraphs.heading: Who writes the words
paragraphs.text: Three modes. Artificial intelligence with a fallback, artificial intelligence only, or your own phrases only.

paragraphs.heading: Your own phrases
paragraphs.text: And this is that fallback. Write a handful in your own voice and it will use them when it cannot do better.

paragraphs.heading: How it should sound
paragraphs.text: You can steer the tone and the length, so it does not read like a robot being enthusiastic.

paragraphs.heading: Caps that keep you safe
paragraphs.text: Now the limits. Per run, per day, and a lifetime total. These are the difference between engaged and reported.

paragraphs.heading: And a pause between them
paragraphs.text: Plus a wait between comments, with a bit of randomness so it is not metronomic.

paragraphs.heading: The box that decides everything
paragraphs.text: Here is the important one. Dry run. Ticked, it writes comments to a log and posts nothing.

paragraphs.heading: Untick it and it is real
paragraphs.text: Untick it and every comment goes live on a stranger's list, under your name, with no confirmation.

paragraphs.heading: Read the log first
paragraphs.text: So do this. Run it in dry run, read what it wrote, and only then decide whether you would have posted it.

paragraphs.heading: Then Start
paragraphs.text: That is the button. Nothing is pressed today, because the browser this opens is signed into a real account.

paragraphs.heading: On a timer
paragraphs.text: And like its sibling, it can run on a schedule once you trust what it writes.

paragraphs.heading: Keeping the record
paragraphs.text: History can be saved out, and clearing it can be undone, which is more than most things here offer.

paragraphs.heading: So, the order
paragraphs.text: Dry run for a week. Read every comment. Then untick the box and start with five a day.

WK5FRSje3qg.title: Get Noticed On Benable: Benable Like Butler

paragraphs.heading: How people find you
paragraphs.text: On Benable, liking someone's list puts your name in front of them. It is the polite knock on the door.

paragraphs.heading: Doing it by hand is tedious
paragraphs.text: Thirty profiles, each with a dozen collections. That is an hour of clicking hearts.

paragraphs.heading: So it does the clicking
paragraphs.text: You give it a list of profiles. It opens a browser, walks each one, and taps the hearts.

paragraphs.heading: These are real likes
paragraphs.text: Which means they are real. They show up in real notifications, and this app cannot take them back.

paragraphs.heading: Who to visit
paragraphs.text: Start here. Paste in the profile links of creators you actually want to be seen by.

paragraphs.heading: Add as many as you like
paragraphs.text: And add another row whenever you find someone new worth following.

paragraphs.heading: How many per visit
paragraphs.text: Now the pacing. Cap how many hearts it taps in one run. Start low.

paragraphs.heading: And how fast
paragraphs.text: And leave a gap between them, because a hundred likes in a minute does not look like a person.

paragraphs.heading: Three speeds
paragraphs.text: If you would rather not think about it, there are three presets. Careful is the one I would pick.

paragraphs.heading: What to like
paragraphs.text: You can like the collections themselves, the items inside them, or both.

paragraphs.heading: Do not go too deep
paragraphs.text: And cap how many items inside each collection, or one big list eats your whole run.

paragraphs.heading: Skipping what you did before
paragraphs.text: This one decides whether it re-taps things it has already liked. Leave it off and it only does new ones.

paragraphs.heading: You will see it work
paragraphs.text: The browser is always visible for this tool. There is no hidden mode, by design.

paragraphs.heading: Then Start
paragraphs.text: And that is the button. Nothing is pressed here, because these would be real likes on real accounts.

paragraphs.heading: On a schedule
paragraphs.text: You can also set it going on its own. A start time, and how often to repeat.

paragraphs.heading: Turning it on and off
paragraphs.text: Enable arms it. Stop schedule disarms it. Both take effect immediately.

paragraphs.heading: What it has done
paragraphs.text: Underneath is the record. Who you liked, what you liked, and when.

paragraphs.heading: Take it with you
paragraphs.text: And you can save that out as a spreadsheet if you want to keep score.

paragraphs.heading: Clearing is recoverable
paragraphs.text: Clearing the history is one of the rare things in this app you can undo. The undo button appears right after.

paragraphs.heading: Reset means reset
paragraphs.text: Reset total is the heavier one. It asks first, and it clears everything.

paragraphs.heading: So, my advice
paragraphs.text: Ten profiles, careful speed, twenty likes a run, once a day. Slow and steady looks like a person.

nVjf9eA4-mk.title: Catch Deals On Your Own Storefront: Black Friday Butler

paragraphs.heading: Deals move fast
paragraphs.text: A Black Friday price on one of your products might last four hours. If you miss it, you miss the post.

paragraphs.heading: This one just watches
paragraphs.text: Black Friday Butler reads your own storefront on a timer and writes down anything flagged as a deal.

paragraphs.heading: It does not post anything
paragraphs.text: And that is all it does. Despite what the sidebar says, there is no posting here. It finds and it logs.

paragraphs.heading: Where to find it
paragraphs.text: It lives under Amazon Butler in the sidebar, so open that group first and you will find it in the list.

paragraphs.heading: Is it running?
paragraphs.text: This tells you the truth about what it is doing. Idle means nothing is happening right now.

paragraphs.heading: Your storefront link
paragraphs.text: One thing to fill in. Paste the public link to your own Amazon storefront here.

paragraphs.heading: How often to look
paragraphs.text: Then choose how often it re-checks. Manual means only when you press the button.

paragraphs.heading: During the sale, go tighter
paragraphs.text: In a normal week, daily is plenty. On the actual Black Friday weekend, drop it right down.

paragraphs.heading: The box that matters
paragraphs.text: Now the important one. Watch it run opens a real browser window, signed into your Amazon account.

paragraphs.heading: And it is on by default
paragraphs.text: It ships ticked. If you are recording your screen, or anyone is watching, untick it first.

paragraphs.heading: Leave this at zero
paragraphs.text: Slow-mo is a debugging field. It just adds a pause between steps. Zero is right.

paragraphs.heading: Then Start
paragraphs.text: Start does the scan. Nothing is pressed in this video, because it opens that signed-in window.

paragraphs.heading: One thing about Start
paragraphs.text: And here is a catch. Starting a run deletes the previous run's exported file first, before it scans.

paragraphs.heading: So export as you go
paragraphs.text: Which is why you export before you re-run. This saves the table as a spreadsheet.

paragraphs.heading: Or just copy it
paragraphs.text: Or copy the whole table to the clipboard, which is quicker if you are pasting into a caption.

paragraphs.heading: Stopping is safe
paragraphs.text: Stop just ends the run. Nothing you already found is lost.

paragraphs.heading: What you get back
paragraphs.text: And this is the result. One row per deal, with the old price, the new price and the product code.

paragraphs.heading: The one to leave alone
paragraphs.text: Last one. Delete all empties the table and deletes the exported file from your computer too.

paragraphs.heading: So, the short version
paragraphs.text: Paste your storefront, untick watch it run, set it to daily, and check back during the sale.

KhWr6bJPZ-o.title: The Button That Is Not a Check: CC Check

paragraphs.heading: Free money, if you ask
paragraphs.text: Brands run campaigns that pay you extra for products you already talk about. This screen finds them.

paragraphs.heading: One warning first
paragraphs.text: But I need to tell you something before anything else. One button on this page is not what its name says.

paragraphs.heading: This is the one
paragraphs.text: This one. Check ASINs sounds like it just looks. It does not. It says yes to every campaign it finds.

paragraphs.heading: Saying yes is forever
paragraphs.text: Saying yes is a promise to a brand. It also sends them your links. There is no undo, and it never asks first.

paragraphs.heading: This is the safe one
paragraphs.text: So use this one instead while you learn. Check Matches only looks. It cannot accept anything or send anything.

paragraphs.heading: First, give it products
paragraphs.text: It needs to know your products. The easiest way is this button. It copies everything Storefront Butler already found.

paragraphs.heading: Or go get new ones
paragraphs.text: Scan New Content goes back to your storefront and picks up anything you have posted since last time.

paragraphs.heading: Or just paste them
paragraphs.text: You can also paste product codes straight in. One per line, or separated by commas. Either is fine.

paragraphs.heading: Got a gift guide?
paragraphs.text: This one is clever. Paste a link to any page of yours and it pulls every Amazon product out of it.

paragraphs.heading: Now look, safely
paragraphs.text: With products in the table, press Check Matches. This is the safe look I promised. It asks Amazon about every product at once, and it takes a second or two.

paragraphs.heading: Here is what you get
paragraphs.text: Three numbers. How many of your products a brand wants, how many nobody wants yet, and how many campaigns are open.

paragraphs.heading: Nothing has been promised
paragraphs.text: Nothing was accepted there. Nothing was sent. You are just looking at a list, which is exactly where you want to be.

paragraphs.heading: Sort the list
paragraphs.text: Use this to see only the ones with something available, or only the ones you have already said yes to.

paragraphs.heading: Or find one product
paragraphs.text: And this searches the table. Type part of a name or a product code.

paragraphs.heading: When you are ready to say yes
paragraphs.text: Now, when you really do want to accept. Turn this off first, or a browser window opens over whatever you are doing.

vS1HcMwowiA.title: The One That Says Yes For You: Daily Commission Butler

0k7hSllci5w.title: Bulk Delete Old Facebook Posts and Comments Safely

paragraphs.heading: The problem
paragraphs.text: If you have been posting Amazon deals to Facebook for a year or two, you have hundreds of old posts with dead links and expired promo codes still sitting on your timeline. Deleting them by hand is three dots, delete, confirm, scroll, over and over.

paragraphs.heading: What this tool does
paragraphs.text: Delete Posts and Comments does that sweep for you. You describe what should go, it finds every match, and it removes them at a human pace. Before anything else, one thing you need to hear clearly.

paragraphs.heading: Deleting is permanent
paragraphs.text: Facebook deletion is permanent. This tool keeps a history log of everything it removed, but that log is a receipt, not an undo button. There is no restore inside the app. That is exactly why the first button is Preview, not Run.

paragraphs.heading: Set up in Deals Butler first
paragraphs.text: Start with the Facebook profile. This dropdown is not its own list. It is literally the profiles you set up in Deals Butler, and cleanup runs on that profile's signed-in Facebook session. If you have not set one up there, you will only see Default here and the run cannot reach your account.

paragraphs.heading: Where to clean up
paragraphs.text: Next, where to clean. My timeline sweeps your own profile. Facebook groups or pages sweeps places you post into. Watch what changes when I switch it — picking groups opens up a destination list underneath. And worth knowing before you choose: group cleanup removes posts only. Comment cleanup only ever runs on your own timeline.

paragraphs.heading: Pages are skipped here
paragraphs.text: And one the label does not tell you. When you pick groups or pages, the destination list offers both, but the cleanup engine needs a facebook dot com slash groups URL. Tick a page and the run simply logs a skip and moves on. Groups work. Pages do not.

paragraphs.heading: Back to your timeline
paragraphs.text: For the rest of this walkthrough I will stay on my timeline, which is where most people start and the only scope that can clean up comments.

paragraphs.heading: Whose content
paragraphs.text: Whose content narrows it further. My own content is the usual choice. Only posts Influencer Butler published is the surgical one: it reads the record Deals kept when it posted, so it touches exactly what the app put there and nothing you wrote yourself. If Deals has never published, that option stops with nothing to clean up.

paragraphs.heading: Posts, comments, or both
paragraphs.text: Then pick what to remove. Posts, comments, or both. Keep in mind these share a single budget later on, so turning both on does not double what one run will do.

paragraphs.heading: Deal content only
paragraphs.text: Content type is the setting that makes this safe to leave running. Deal content only matches on the fingerprints of an affiliate post: an Amazon link, an amzn dot to or a dot co slash short link, a geni dot us link, the hashtags ad, affiliate, paid link or commission earned, the phrase as an Amazon Associate, use code, promo code, or a percent off. It reads text only. No images, no unfurling links.

paragraphs.heading: Why Any content is risky
paragraphs.text: Which brings up the sharpest edge in this tool. Switch to Any content with no keywords and no age limits, and a post whose text could not be read — a photo-only group card, say — still counts as a match. Your protect list cannot save it, because there is no text to check against. Deal content only is immune to that, since blank text is never deal content.

paragraphs.heading: Narrow it with keywords
paragraphs.text: The two keyword boxes are your scalpel. Only if it contains means a post has to mention one of these to qualify at all. Leave it blank and everything that passed the other filters qualifies.

paragraphs.heading: The protect list always wins
paragraphs.text: Never delete if it contains is the one to fill in first. Anything here is protected outright, and protection beats inclusion every time. A post matching both a protect word and an include word is skipped, not deleted. Put your giveaway posts, your pinned announcements, anything you would be sick to lose, in this box.

paragraphs.heading: Age rules
paragraphs.text: Age is the other honest filter. Only older than lets you sweep anything past its shelf life. Always keep newer than draws a line in front of your recent posts that nothing crosses. Set that second one even if you set nothing else.

paragraphs.heading: Skip pinned posts
paragraphs.text: Skip pinned and featured posts is on by default and there is very little reason to turn it off. Like the protect list, it is an exclusion, so it wins over everything else you have set.

paragraphs.heading: The cap is your real safety net
paragraphs.text: Max deletions per run is the setting that turns a mistake into a small mistake. The label mentions unattended runs, but it caps every run, including the one you start by hand. Posts and comments count against the same number. It defaults to twenty five, the floor is one, and there is deliberately no unlimited option.

paragraphs.heading: Pace it like a person
paragraphs.text: Delay between deletes and the extra random delay keep the run looking human instead of like a script. Eight seconds with a few seconds of jitter is a sensible starting point. Faster is not better here.

paragraphs.heading: Always preview first
paragraphs.text: Now the part that matters. Preview matches does everything a real run does except delete. It opens your timeline, reads each post, applies every filter you just set, and writes what it would have removed into the results table below. Nothing is touched.

paragraphs.heading: Read the results table
paragraphs.text: Read this table before you go any further. Every row is a post the run would have removed, with the snippet and how old it is. If you see something in here you want to keep, do not adjust and hope. Add a word from it to your protect list and preview again.

paragraphs.heading: Preview ignores the cap
paragraphs.text: One thing about preview that surprises people. It ignores the per run cap on purpose, because it is not deleting anything, so it will keep walking through candidates — up to a few hundred. On a big account that takes a while. Stop ends it cleanly whenever you have seen enough.

paragraphs.heading: Tick watch it run, then pause
paragraphs.text: If you want to see it working, tick watch it run and the browser comes on screen. Small but real quirk: that checkbox reaches the run through a save that lands about half a second later. Tick it, take a breath, then press the button. Rush it and the run goes invisible in the background.

paragraphs.heading: Then start the cleanup
paragraphs.text: When the preview looks right, and only then, Start cleanup runs the same pass for real, honouring your cap and your pacing. I am not pressing it here, because this is my live account and I would rather show you the panel than lose the posts.

paragraphs.heading: Put it on a schedule
paragraphs.text: Once you trust your filters, hand it the calendar. Pick a start time, choose how often to repeat, and enable the schedule. Every fire runs inside the same filters and the same cap, so a scheduled sweep can never do more than one manual run would.

paragraphs.heading: The counters are cumulative
paragraphs.text: Last thing to read correctly. These four counters are not a summary of the run you just did. They total your recent history, so they carry over between runs, and a preview bumps matched even though it deleted nothing.

paragraphs.heading: Where to start
paragraphs.text: So, the safe order. Fill in the protect list first. Set always keep newer than. Leave content type on deal content only. Preview, read the table, adjust, preview again. Then start a small capped run. Once two previews in a row look right, put it on a schedule and stop thinking about it.

KvhCr37RiCE.title: Have A Facebook Group Written For You: Facebook Group Builder

paragraphs.text: A Facebook group you own is the one audience nobody can take away. No algorithm between you and them.

paragraphs.text: This does the writing. Names, description, welcome post, a batch of engagement posts, and a cover image.

paragraphs.heading: And then builds it
paragraphs.text: Then it can go and actually create the group on Facebook for you. That is the part to be careful with.

paragraphs.heading: One word to start
paragraphs.text: Everything comes from this. The niche. What the group is about.

paragraphs.heading: How it should sound
paragraphs.text: Then the tone, so the copy sounds like your corner of the internet rather than a press release.

paragraphs.heading: How many, and how private
paragraphs.text: How many groups to plan, and whether they should be public or private.

paragraphs.heading: Name it yourself if you want
paragraphs.text: You can let it invent names, or type your own and it works around that.

paragraphs.heading: How much to write
paragraphs.text: And how many engagement posts to write up front. Ten gives you a fortnight of content.

paragraphs.heading: Then generate
paragraphs.text: This does the thinking. It costs a little of your artificial intelligence credit each time you press it.

paragraphs.heading: Read it before you use it
paragraphs.text: Afterwards a review area appears below with everything it wrote, and you can edit any of it.

paragraphs.heading: The cover image
paragraphs.text: Then the cover. Pick a style, pick a quality, and decide whether the group name goes on the picture.

paragraphs.heading: This one costs more

paragraphs.heading: Which account
paragraphs.text: Now the building part. First, which Facebook login it should use.

paragraphs.heading: The setting that actually matters
paragraphs.text: And this. Assisted fills in Facebook's form and waits for you to press Create yourself. Full auto presses it.

paragraphs.heading: Leave it on assisted
paragraphs.text: Leave it on assisted. That is genuinely the only thing keeping a human in the loop here.

paragraphs.heading: Because this box does nothing
paragraphs.text: Which brings us to this. It says pause for my approval between steps, and it is ticked.

paragraphs.heading: Nothing reads it
paragraphs.text: And nothing reads it. The part that does the building never looks at this box. It has no effect at all.

paragraphs.heading: A sensible daily limit
paragraphs.text: This one is real though. How many new groups it may create in a day. Two is the default.

paragraphs.heading: Then Build
paragraphs.text: And that is Build. Not pressed here, because in full auto it would make a real group on a real account.

paragraphs.heading: Watch the button, not the badge
paragraphs.text: One oddity. The status badge never changes. A stop button appears while it works, and that is your real signal.

paragraphs.heading: Keeping it alive
paragraphs.text: Open this and there is more. Recurring posts to keep the group busy, and inviting people who react.

paragraphs.heading: How often to post
paragraphs.text: How many posts a week, and roughly what time of day they should land.

paragraphs.heading: Inviting the reactors
paragraphs.text: And this invites people who engage with those posts to join. Same pacing settings you would expect.

paragraphs.heading: Then hand it to deals
paragraphs.text: Once a group exists it shows up in a table below, and you can point a deals workspace at it.

paragraphs.heading: So, the order
paragraphs.text: Niche, generate, read what it wrote, generate a cover, then build one group on assisted and press Create yourself.

fIpsl8kimOs.title: Turn Group Reactions Into Page Followers: Facebook Inviter

paragraphs.heading: Reactions are wasted
paragraphs.text: You post a deal in a group. Forty people react. And then nothing, because none of them follow your page.

paragraphs.heading: This chases them up
paragraphs.text: Facebook Inviter opens each of those reaction lists and invites every one of those people to follow you.

paragraphs.heading: Nothing is running
paragraphs.text: This badge is honest. Idle now, and it goes to running when something is happening.

paragraphs.heading: The one required field
paragraphs.text: One thing it needs. The numeric identifier of the page or profile you want people to follow.

paragraphs.heading: Groups to leave out
paragraphs.text: Then any groups to skip. Somewhere you are a member but would rather not be seen inviting people.

paragraphs.heading: How many per post
paragraphs.text: Now the cap, and this one matters. Zero here means unlimited, which is not what you want on your first run.

paragraphs.heading: How far to scroll
paragraphs.text: And how hard to dig into each group. Ten scrolls is plenty.

paragraphs.heading: Untick this
paragraphs.text: Watch it run brings the automation browser to the front, on top of whatever you are doing.

paragraphs.heading: Then Start
paragraphs.text: And that is Start. It is not pressed here, because every invite it sends is real and cannot be recalled.

paragraphs.heading: There is no practice run
paragraphs.text: There is no preview and no dry run in this tool. Nothing between the button and real invites.

paragraphs.heading: Or set it going daily
paragraphs.text: You can also schedule it. A start time and how many days between runs.

paragraphs.heading: Arming it
paragraphs.text: Enable turns the schedule on. It will not let you arm it without the profile identifier filled in.

paragraphs.heading: Turning it off
paragraphs.text: And stop schedule disarms it, which is safe to press at any time.

paragraphs.heading: When it last went
paragraphs.text: These two lines tell you when it last ran and when it will run next.

paragraphs.heading: Watching it work
paragraphs.text: And the log underneath is where you see what it is doing, group by group, as it works.

paragraphs.heading: So, when it lands
paragraphs.text: Set a small per post cap, one run, then go and look at your follower count before you widen anything.

F0zedlQ9x5Y.title: Find Brands That Already Pay Creators: Goldmine Butler

paragraphs.heading: The shortcut to a pitch list
paragraphs.text: The easiest brands to pitch are the ones already paying someone like you. This finds them.

paragraphs.heading: How it works
paragraphs.text: You give it links to other creators' Amazon shops. It reads their posts looking for sponsored ones.

paragraphs.heading: Then it names the brand
paragraphs.text: For every sponsored post it finds, it looks up who makes the product. That is your list.

paragraphs.heading: It only reads
paragraphs.text: Nothing here messages anybody or touches your account. It reads public pages, the same as you could.

paragraphs.heading: Paste the shop links
paragraphs.text: Start here. Paste the address of a creator's Amazon shop. Pick people in your own niche.

paragraphs.heading: Add a few more
paragraphs.text: This adds another box. Five or six creators gives you plenty to work with.

paragraphs.heading: Narrow it down
paragraphs.text: Keywords keep it focused. Type a word and press Add, and it only keeps posts mentioning it.

paragraphs.heading: Cap the work
paragraphs.text: And this caps how many posts it reads per shop. Leave it low the first time.

paragraphs.heading: One thing to know first
paragraphs.text: Before you press Run, know this. It clears your last set of results first, with no warning.

paragraphs.heading: So export first
paragraphs.text: So if the last run found something good, export it before you run again.

paragraphs.heading: Ignore this box
paragraphs.text: And ignore this tick box. It promises to show you a browser window. It does nothing at all.

paragraphs.heading: Then it works quietly
paragraphs.text: Press Run and it goes off quietly. This line tells you what it is doing.

paragraphs.heading: Four numbers
paragraphs.text: These count up. Shops read, sponsored posts found, products, and brands. Brands is the one you care about.

paragraphs.heading: Here is what you get
paragraphs.text: And this is the table. One row per sponsored post, with the brand who paid for it.

paragraphs.heading: Sort it your way
paragraphs.text: Click a heading to sort. Grouping by brand shows you who is spending the most on creators.

paragraphs.heading: Find one
paragraphs.text: Or search. It matches brands, product codes, titles, and the shop it came from.

paragraphs.heading: Take it away
paragraphs.text: Export gives you the lot as a spreadsheet. Note that it saves everything, not just what you filtered to.

paragraphs.heading: Careful here
paragraphs.text: Last warning. Delete All empties the table and forgets it permanently. It does not ask.

paragraphs.heading: So, the routine
paragraphs.text: Six shops, a keyword, twenty five posts each. Run it, sort by brand, and start writing emails.

0Db0me3aaS4.title: Fill Your Facebook Group From An Email List: Group Invite Butler

paragraphs.heading: The empty group
paragraphs.text: You made a Facebook group. It has four members and two of them are you on different accounts.

paragraphs.heading: And you have a list
paragraphs.text: Meanwhile the Goldmine tools have collected a few hundred email addresses of people in your niche.

paragraphs.heading: This joins the two
paragraphs.text: Group Invite Butler works through that list and invites each address to your group, one at a time.

paragraphs.heading: One at a time matters
paragraphs.text: One at a time, with a pause. Facebook notices bursts, and a burst is how accounts get limited.

paragraphs.heading: Nothing is running
paragraphs.text: This badge tells you the truth. Idle means no invites are going out.

paragraphs.heading: Which group
paragraphs.text: First, the group. Paste its address here. This is the only required field.

paragraphs.heading: Where the list comes from
paragraphs.text: Then the queue. Load a spreadsheet of addresses if you already have one.

paragraphs.heading: Or just paste some
paragraphs.text: Or open this and paste them straight in, which is quicker for a handful.

paragraphs.heading: Add them to the queue
paragraphs.text: Paste, press add, and they join the pending list below.

paragraphs.heading: The pacing, which is everything
paragraphs.text: Now the important part. Seconds between invites. Forty five is the default and it is sensible.

paragraphs.heading: And some randomness
paragraphs.text: Plus a random extra few seconds, so the gaps are not identical. That is what makes it look human.

paragraphs.heading: A ceiling per day
paragraphs.text: Then a daily cap. Thirty is the default. Resist the urge to make it three hundred.

paragraphs.heading: And per run
paragraphs.text: And a per run cap, for when you want a short burst and then a long rest.

paragraphs.heading: Retrying failures
paragraphs.text: This is off by default. Turned on, it quietly tries failed addresses again later.

paragraphs.heading: Untick this
paragraphs.text: And this opens the browser window in front of you. Untick it for an unattended run.

paragraphs.heading: Then Start
paragraphs.text: That is Start. Not pressed here, because these are real invites to real people.

paragraphs.heading: On a schedule
paragraphs.text: Or set it going on a repeat, so a few invites go out every day without you.

paragraphs.heading: How often
paragraphs.text: Pick an interval here. Choose custom and a box appears for your own number of hours.

paragraphs.heading: Arming it
paragraphs.text: Enable arms the schedule, stop schedule disarms it.

paragraphs.heading: Reading the queue
paragraphs.text: The table underneath is your queue. Address, name, where it came from, and whether it has gone yet.

paragraphs.heading: Two buttons that appear later
paragraphs.text: Once things have failed or sent, two more buttons show up. Retry failed, and redo sent.

paragraphs.heading: Careful with redo
paragraphs.text: Redo sent puts people you have already invited back in the queue. They get invited a second time.

paragraphs.heading: And this one does not ask
paragraphs.text: Last warning. Clear queue empties the whole pending list, with no confirmation and no way back.

paragraphs.heading: Save it first
paragraphs.text: Which is why you export first. This writes the whole queue out as a spreadsheet.

paragraphs.heading: So, my advice
paragraphs.text: Twenty addresses, forty five second gap, thirty a day. Watch the first run, then leave it alone.

fOyidT7HXEI.title: Pull Brand Emails Out Of Your DMs: Instagram Email Collection

paragraphs.heading: It is in there somewhere
paragraphs.text: A brand messaged you three months ago with their email address. You know it is in your inbox. Good luck finding it.

paragraphs.heading: This goes and finds them
paragraphs.text: So this reads your Instagram messages and pulls out every email address anybody has ever typed at you.

paragraphs.text: Worth being clear. It sends nothing and replies to nothing. It reads your own inbox and writes a list.

paragraphs.heading: Nothing is running
paragraphs.text: This badge is the honest one. Idle means nothing is happening right now.

paragraphs.heading: How deep to go
paragraphs.text: First setting. How many conversations to look through. Leave it empty and it does the whole inbox.

paragraphs.heading: Only the new ones
paragraphs.text: This is ticked already, and you want it ticked. It only looks at messages newer than your last run.

paragraphs.heading: The slow, thorough option
paragraphs.text: This one scrolls back through each conversation properly. Much slower. Worth it once, on your first run.

paragraphs.heading: Untick this one
paragraphs.text: And this. Watch it run opens a browser window showing your actual Instagram inbox. Untick it before you start.

paragraphs.heading: Then Run
paragraphs.text: Then Run does the work. It is not pressed here, because it opens my real inbox.

paragraphs.heading: Run is also stop
paragraphs.text: Once it is going, that same button says Stop. You can end it any time and keep what it found.

paragraphs.text: Open this and you can put it on a schedule, so new addresses just appear without you thinking about it.

paragraphs.text: Pick how often, apply it, and it runs on its own. Stop schedule turns it back off.

paragraphs.text: The result is a table. Who messaged you, the address they gave, and when.

paragraphs.heading: Finding one

paragraphs.heading: Keeping track of replies
paragraphs.text: And you can mark each one as sent once you have followed up, then filter to only the ones you have not.

paragraphs.text: Once rows exist, a toolbar appears above the table. Copy the lot, or export it as a spreadsheet.

paragraphs.heading: Deleting is safe here
paragraphs.text: And unusually for this app, the delete buttons in that toolbar both ask you first and both save a snapshot.

paragraphs.heading: Which this brings back
paragraphs.text: So if you delete the wrong thing, this button puts it back. Very few tools here offer that.

paragraphs.heading: So, the routine
paragraphs.text: Untick watch it run, do one full scan with history on, then put it on a weekly schedule and forget about it.

d5nzVFOI2lc.title: Find Brands That Pay Creators: Instagram Goldmine

paragraphs.heading: The question this answers
paragraphs.text: Which brands are actually paying creators like you right now? Not last year. This month. That is the whole question.

paragraphs.heading: How it finds them
paragraphs.text: Instagram Goldmine reads public posts and looks for paid ones. Then it tells you who paid, and how to reach them.

paragraphs.heading: It only looks
paragraphs.text: One thing to be clear about. This tool only reads. It never follows, likes, comments, or messages anybody.

paragraphs.heading: Sign in first
paragraphs.text: Instagram hides most of this from strangers. So click here first and sign in. It opens a normal Chrome window. Tick trust this device, then close it. Every Instagram tool in the app shares that one sign in.

paragraphs.heading: Start with creators like you
paragraphs.text: Now the important part. Type a few creators who post the kind of thing you post. One name per line.

paragraphs.heading: These are called seeds
paragraphs.text: Those names are your seeds. The app starts at each one and works outward from there.

paragraphs.heading: How wide it should go
paragraphs.text: Run mode decides how far it wanders. Seeds plus suggested is the one most people want. It checks your names, then who Instagram says is similar.

paragraphs.heading: How big is big enough
paragraphs.text: Min followers sets the floor. Fifty thousand is a decent starting point. Below that, brands are usually not paying yet.

paragraphs.heading: How far past each seed
paragraphs.text: Max suggested per seed decides how far it wanders from each name. Twenty five is a sensible first try.

paragraphs.heading: Keep the first run small
paragraphs.text: Max profiles per run is your brake. Set it low the first time. Twenty five is plenty to see if this is working.

paragraphs.heading: Or stop at a number of emails
paragraphs.text: This one is nicer. Stop after this many emails. It quits as soon as it has what you asked for.

paragraphs.heading: Only recent posts
paragraphs.text: Set this to thirty and it ignores anything older than a month. Old deals are not much use to you.

paragraphs.heading: What counts as paid
paragraphs.text: Now, what makes a post count. Tick this and it only keeps posts that say hashtag ad, or sponsored.

paragraphs.heading: The label Instagram adds itself
paragraphs.text: This one is stronger. Paid partnership is a label Instagram puts on. A creator cannot fake it.

paragraphs.heading: Go slower, get blocked less
paragraphs.text: Turn on safe mode. It waits twice as long between pages. It takes longer, but Instagram stays happy.

paragraphs.heading: Chase the email in the bio
paragraphs.text: This one is worth turning on. If a creator hides their email behind a link, the app opens it and looks.

paragraphs.heading: It remembers who it checked
paragraphs.text: The app skips anyone it looked at in the last two weeks. Tick this only if you want it to look again anyway.

paragraphs.heading: Then press this
paragraphs.text: That is the setup. Start Discovery kicks it off. A Chrome window opens and does the reading for you.

paragraphs.heading: Watch these three numbers
paragraphs.text: These three count up while it works. Profiles looked at, posts read, and the ones that actually qualified.

paragraphs.heading: Here is what you get
paragraphs.text: And this is the payoff. Every row is one paid post. The creator, the brand that paid them, and an email.

paragraphs.heading: The column that matters
paragraphs.text: Look at the brand email column. That is a real inbox at a company that already pays people to post.

paragraphs.heading: Send them straight to Pitch Butler
paragraphs.text: Tick the rows you like, then send them to Pitch Butler. It writes the email and tracks who replied.

paragraphs.heading: Or take it with you
paragraphs.text: Prefer a spreadsheet? Export CSV drops the whole table into a file you can open anywhere.

paragraphs.heading: Careful with this one
paragraphs.text: One warning. Clear results empties the table and forgets everyone it checked. There is no undo and no are you sure.

paragraphs.heading: Hashtags instead of people
paragraphs.text: One last mode. Switch run mode to hashtags and it hunts by topic instead of by creator.

paragraphs.heading: Then type your topics
paragraphs.text: Type the hashtags your buyers actually follow. The app reads those posts and collects the creators behind them.

paragraphs.heading: Where to start
paragraphs.text: So: sign in, add three creators, cap it at twenty five, and press Start. You will have a brand list before lunch.

lak0Ggx3mH0.title: Stay Visible To The Accounts That Matter: Instagram Like Butler

paragraphs.heading: Being remembered
paragraphs.text: There are twenty brands and creators you want to stay visible to. Liking their posts works. Remembering to do it does not.

paragraphs.heading: So it does the rounds
paragraphs.text: You give it a list of accounts. It visits each one, looks at their recent posts, and taps the heart.

paragraphs.heading: These are real likes
paragraphs.text: Real likes, on real accounts, from your account. They land in real notifications and this app cannot take them back.

paragraphs.heading: And there is no practice mode
paragraphs.text: There is no dry run button here either. Pressing start means liking things.

paragraphs.heading: Who to visit
paragraphs.text: Start with the list. Usernames or profile links, one per line.

paragraphs.heading: Adding more
paragraphs.text: And add a row whenever you spot someone else worth keeping warm.

paragraphs.heading: How many per round
paragraphs.text: Then the ceiling. How many hearts in one run. Twenty is plenty to start.

paragraphs.heading: How fast
paragraphs.text: And the gap between them. A few seconds is not a person. Give it longer.

paragraphs.heading: Or pick a preset
paragraphs.text: If you would rather not think about it, there are three speeds. Careful is the one I would choose.

paragraphs.heading: How deep per account
paragraphs.text: This caps how many of each account's posts it touches. Three or four is enough to be noticed.

paragraphs.heading: Repeat visits
paragraphs.text: This decides whether it likes posts it has already liked. Untick it and it only ever does new ones.

paragraphs.heading: Untick this too
paragraphs.text: And this opens a browser window on your real Instagram. Untick it unless you want to watch.

paragraphs.heading: Then Start
paragraphs.text: That is the button. Not pressed here, for the reason we started with.

paragraphs.heading: Pausing
paragraphs.text: Pause holds it where it is. A stop button appears beside it once something is actually going.

paragraphs.heading: On a timer
paragraphs.text: And it can look after itself. A start time and how often to repeat.

paragraphs.heading: Arming the schedule
paragraphs.text: Save arms it, cancel disarms it. While a schedule is on, the manual buttons lock so the two cannot collide.

paragraphs.heading: What it has done
paragraphs.text: Underneath, the log. Which account, which post, and when.

paragraphs.heading: Save it out
paragraphs.text: Download gives you the whole thing as a spreadsheet.

paragraphs.heading: Two kinds of clearing
paragraphs.text: Clear selected removes some rows. Clear all removes the lot. Both ask you first.

paragraphs.heading: And the heavy one
paragraphs.text: Reset total is the one to be careful with. It asks, and its warning is the strongest in the panel.

paragraphs.heading: So, my advice
paragraphs.text: Fifteen accounts, careful speed, three posts each, once a day. That looks like somebody scrolling.

vkHWnPDKc9s.title: Get Noticed by Other Creators: Like Butler

paragraphs.heading: Why bother liking
paragraphs.text: Other creators see who likes their posts. Show up enough and they start recognising your name.

paragraphs.heading: What it actually does
paragraphs.text: Ignore the tooltip on the menu, it is wrong. This does not touch campaigns or brands at all.

paragraphs.heading: It likes creators' posts
paragraphs.text: You give it links to other people's Amazon shops. It opens each one and taps the heart on their posts.

paragraphs.heading: A real like, on your account
paragraphs.text: Those are real likes, from your real account. Which is why I am not pressing anything today.

paragraphs.heading: There is no undo
paragraphs.text: There is no unlike button here, and no practice mode. Once a heart is tapped, that is that.

paragraphs.heading: Start with the links
paragraphs.text: So, the setup. Paste the address of a creator's Amazon shop page here. Add as many as you like.

paragraphs.heading: Add another
paragraphs.text: This adds another box. Five or ten creators in your niche is a sensible starting list.

paragraphs.heading: The most important box
paragraphs.text: Now the one that matters most. Max likes per run. Leave it empty and it means unlimited. Do not leave it empty.

paragraphs.heading: Go slowly
paragraphs.text: And this is the gap between each like. Longer is safer. Amazon notices things that move too fast.

paragraphs.heading: Three shortcuts
paragraphs.text: These three just fill that box for you. Careful is fifteen seconds, and careful is the right answer.

paragraphs.heading: Do not repeat yourself
paragraphs.text: This remembers who you already liked. The cooldown is how many days before it visits them again.

paragraphs.heading: Or ignore the memory
paragraphs.text: Ticking this ignores all that and taps every heart again. Rarely what you want.

paragraphs.heading: Pick what to like
paragraphs.text: You can also choose the kind of post. Videos only, or photos, or their idea lists.

paragraphs.heading: Watch the first one
paragraphs.text: Leave this on for your first run. A browser opens so you can actually see it working.

paragraphs.heading: This is the real one
paragraphs.text: And this starts it. Real hearts, on real posts, straight away. No question first.

paragraphs.heading: How to tell it is running
paragraphs.text: While it goes, the Start button is replaced by a Stop button. That swap is your signal.

paragraphs.heading: A button that lies
paragraphs.text: Watch out for this one. It says reset the counter. It actually stops the whole run.

paragraphs.heading: What it has done
paragraphs.text: Underneath is the record. Which creators you liked and when, so you are not guessing.

paragraphs.heading: Set it and forget it
paragraphs.text: You can put it on a timer too. Fair warning: once the timer is on, the buttons above go dead.

paragraphs.heading: So, my advice
paragraphs.text: Five creators, twenty likes, fifteen seconds apart. Watch the first run. Then leave it alone.

ktfU-gayYFU.title: What Should I Film Next?: Orders Butler

paragraphs.heading: The daily question
paragraphs.text: You have hundreds of things in your house you already bought. Which one should you film today?

paragraphs.heading: It reads your own orders
paragraphs.text: Orders Butler opens Amazon and reads your order history. Everything you bought, what you paid, and what it pays you.

paragraphs.heading: Only your account, only reading
paragraphs.text: It only ever reads. It never buys anything, never returns anything, and never touches anyone else's account.

paragraphs.heading: Your first run
paragraphs.text: If your table is empty, this button is all you need. It starts the first read of your order history.

paragraphs.heading: Turn this off first
paragraphs.text: Before that though, untick this. Left on, a browser window opens in front of you and sits there the whole time.

paragraphs.heading: Leave this one on
paragraphs.text: This one you keep. Skipping pictures makes the read much faster, and you were never going to look at them.

paragraphs.heading: How far back to go
paragraphs.text: Now, how much history. Only new since last run is the right choice almost every time. It stops as soon as it recognises orders.

paragraphs.heading: The first time only
paragraphs.text: The very first time, pick all years instead. It walks back to twenty thirteen. It is slow, and you only do it once.

paragraphs.heading: A trap in the third option
paragraphs.text: Careful with this one. Choose selected years but tick no years, and it quietly reads everything instead of nothing.

paragraphs.heading: Then press Run
paragraphs.text: Then press Run and leave it. A long history can take a while, so start it and go do something else.

paragraphs.heading: How to tell it is working
paragraphs.text: Watch this little badge, not the Stop button. The badge tells you the truth about what it is doing.

paragraphs.heading: Here is what you get
paragraphs.text: And this is the result. One row for everything you bought, with what you paid and what you earn beside it.

paragraphs.heading: The column that decides
paragraphs.text: The content column is the one that matters. It shows whether you already have a photo or a video for each product. These are the real orders you made, and exactly what is still missing to film.

paragraphs.heading: The one button to remember
paragraphs.text: Now the best button in the app. Film these first sorts everything by what is actually worth your afternoon.

paragraphs.heading: How it picks
paragraphs.text: It favours things that pay well, that people are buying, and that hardly anyone has filmed yet.

paragraphs.heading: Tune it to you
paragraphs.text: You can move those goalposts. Or press reset if you fiddle too much and want the sensible numbers back.

paragraphs.heading: The columns worth knowing
paragraphs.text: Slide across and the table tells you more about each product. Its sales rank, how many other creators have already filmed it, whether it shows in a carousel, and roughly how many sell a month.

paragraphs.heading: Just the gaps
paragraphs.text: You can also filter to the gaps. Show me only the things still missing a photo.

paragraphs.heading: Select what to shoot
paragraphs.text: Tick the ones you want, or select them all at once.

paragraphs.heading: A list for your film day
paragraphs.text: Then print a checklist of exactly what to shoot, with a box to tick off each item as you go.

paragraphs.heading: Your filming checklist
paragraphs.text: And here is the checklist it makes. One line for every product you picked, with its photo and a box to tick off as you film it.

paragraphs.heading: Hand it to the next tool
paragraphs.text: Or send them straight to Content Butler, which writes the posts from what you filmed.

paragraphs.heading: One thing about export
paragraphs.text: Export gives you a spreadsheet of everything. Worth knowing it is there.

paragraphs.heading: So, the short version
paragraphs.text: Untick the watch box, choose all years, press Run once. After that, press film these first and go shoot.

YoJadCTQFFg.title: Copy Your Photos Everywhere: Photo Reload Butler

paragraphs.heading: Same idea, for pictures
paragraphs.text: This is the photo version of Video Reload. Same job, same shape, one important difference.

paragraphs.heading: It reads one shop
paragraphs.text: It reads the photos on one storefront and posts copies to the other countries you pick.

paragraphs.heading: Here is the difference
paragraphs.text: And here is the difference, which matters more than anything else on this screen.

paragraphs.heading: Nothing asks you first
paragraphs.text: The video one makes you type the word delete before it removes anything. This one never asks. At all.

paragraphs.heading: Not even for deleting
paragraphs.text: Not for posting, and not for delete only mode either. You press it, and it happens.

paragraphs.heading: So triple check
paragraphs.text: Which is why you check every setting twice before that button. Let us go through them.

paragraphs.heading: Where it reads from
paragraphs.text: Source is the shop it copies from. One country, usually your main one.

fN26bxHT-bw.title: Fix Every Old Affiliate Link At Once: Relink Butler

paragraphs.text: You change link provider, or you get a new tag. Every link you have ever posted is now the old one.

paragraphs.text: YouTube, Pinterest and Benable all need a real browser signed into your account to edit a published post.

paragraphs.text: Then Preview. This is the safe one. It reads, works out the swap, and writes nothing anywhere.

paragraphs.heading: Read the table
paragraphs.text: Afterwards you get a row per link. The old one on the left, the proposed one on the right.

paragraphs.text: And here is the thing to know. Nothing is ticked for you. You approve each row you want, one at a time.

upRAOn8Ebdk.title: Write Amazon Video Scripts in One Click

paragraphs.heading: The blank page problem
paragraphs.text: You have the product in your hand. The camera is ready. And you have no idea what to say for 30 seconds.

paragraphs.heading: What this tool makes
paragraphs.text: Voiceover Butler writes that script for you. One important thing first, because the name fools people.

paragraphs.heading: It writes words, not audio
paragraphs.text: This tool does not make a voice. It makes words on a page for you to read out loud. Nothing here records audio. You are still the voice.

paragraphs.heading: Add your product
paragraphs.text: Start here. Paste the ASIN of the product you are filming. That is the code Amazon gives every item. One per line if you have a few.

paragraphs.heading: No ASIN? No problem
paragraphs.text: Selling something that is not on Amazon? Switch to the second button and type the product in by hand instead.

paragraphs.heading: How long is your video?
paragraphs.text: Now tell it how long to write for. 30 seconds is a good place to start. Anything under 5 or over 120 gets pulled back to fit.

paragraphs.heading: Pick the kind of video
paragraphs.text: Video type changes the whole shape of the script. An unboxing sounds nothing like a tutorial. Pick the one you are actually filming.

paragraphs.heading: Pick your first line
paragraphs.text: The opening hook is your first sentence. It is the one that decides if someone keeps watching. Pick a style, or write your own.

paragraphs.heading: How fast you talk
paragraphs.text: Pacing is just how fast you talk. Fast and punchy fits more words into the same 30 seconds. Slow gives each one room.

paragraphs.heading: Say how you got it
paragraphs.text: This one matters. If a brand sent you the product free, or you earn from the link, you have to say so out loud. Pick which one is true for you.

paragraphs.heading: But check that line yourself
paragraphs.text: One honest warning. The tool asks the writer to add that line, but nothing here checks that it really did. Read your script and make sure the line is there.

paragraphs.heading: Tell it what to lean on
paragraphs.text: Notes is where you steer it. One line about the angle you want. It reads this and builds the script around it.

paragraphs.heading: Match the script to your shots
paragraphs.text: If you already know your shots, list them here with rough times. The words will then line up with what is on screen.

paragraphs.heading: Brand rules go here
paragraphs.text: Did a brand send you rules to follow? Paste them here, or load their PDF. The writer treats them as rules it must obey.

paragraphs.heading: Add it to the list
paragraphs.text: Add to queue puts it in the list below. Nothing has been written yet, and nothing has cost you anything yet.

paragraphs.heading: Set it once, not every time
paragraphs.text: Before you do a lot of these, open Settings. Everything you set in there fills this form in for you next time.

paragraphs.heading: The gotcha with the queue
paragraphs.text: Here is the one that catches people out. Add 10 products with 10 different setups, and they do not each keep their own. Whatever the form says when you press Generate is what every one of them gets.

paragraphs.heading: So do them in groups
paragraphs.text: So work in groups. Set the form for unboxings, generate all your unboxings, then change the form and do the tutorials.

paragraphs.heading: Generate costs money
paragraphs.text: Generate is the button that spends money. Each one is a paid call to OpenAI using your own key. Adding to the queue is free. This part is not.

paragraphs.heading: Set your key up first
paragraphs.text: That key lives in API Integrations, over in the left menu. No key, no script. Set it up once before you start.

paragraphs.heading: The rule checker
paragraphs.text: Every script gets checked against Amazon's rules before you see it. No prices, no emojis, no brand names, no cure claims, no buy now.

paragraphs.heading: A rejected script still costs you
paragraphs.text: If it breaks a rule, the script is thrown away and the job turns red. You still paid for it. Fix your notes and try again.

paragraphs.heading: Open it and read it
paragraphs.text: When it is done, click View to open the finished script. Read it before you film. You can edit any line right here if it does not sound like you.

paragraphs.heading: Deleting cannot be undone
paragraphs.text: Careful with delete. Removing a job also removes every script it wrote. There is no undo and no trash can.

paragraphs.heading: Where your scripts turn up
paragraphs.text: Your scripts follow you to Orders Butler. Tick include voiceover scripts on the content checklist, and each one prints next to its product.

paragraphs.heading: Where to start
paragraphs.text: So the short version. Add your key. Fill in Settings once. Queue one product, generate it, and read what you get. Then do the rest in groups.

vK0i1Zj0AKc.title: Get Your Videos Onto YouTube: YouTube Butler

paragraphs.heading: Videos you already have
paragraphs.text: You have made dozens of product videos. They are sitting on Amazon doing one job.

paragraphs.heading: A second home for them
paragraphs.text: YouTube is a second audience for the same work. This uploads them for you, with links.

paragraphs.heading: Read this before pressing
paragraphs.text: One warning up front, because it is a big one. The upload button posts publicly, straight away.

paragraphs.heading: Public is the default
paragraphs.text: And the visibility setting comes set to Public out of the box. Change it before you ever run this.

paragraphs.heading: Start with what you have
paragraphs.text: Right. This pulls in the videos your other butlers already made. Completely safe.

paragraphs.heading: Here is your library
paragraphs.text: And there they are. Every video, which product it is for, and whether it has gone up yet.

paragraphs.heading: Four numbers
paragraphs.text: These track the whole job. How many you have, queued, uploaded, and how many failed.

paragraphs.heading: Find the right ones
paragraphs.text: Filter by upright or wide, or by whether they are already done.

paragraphs.heading: Line them up
paragraphs.text: Tick some and queue them. That only marks them. Nothing uploads yet.

paragraphs.heading: Delete is not undo
paragraphs.text: Careful with the delete button beside it though. It asks nothing, and unqueue will not bring them back.

paragraphs.heading: Your videos stay put
paragraphs.text: It only forgets them from this list. The actual video files stay on your computer.

paragraphs.heading: Write it once
paragraphs.text: The templates write every title and description for you. Put your link in here once.

paragraphs.heading: How many at a time
paragraphs.text: And cap how many go up per session. Ten is sensible. It lets you take fifty, which is asking for trouble.

paragraphs.heading: Connecting your channel
paragraphs.text: Connecting YouTube is a five step setup wizard on this tab. Fair warning, those buttons are currently broken.

paragraphs.heading: Then this is the one
paragraphs.text: And this is the button that does it. Upload Queued sounds like a list. It is the publish button.

paragraphs.heading: Not on camera
paragraphs.text: Which is why I am not pressing it. Set your visibility, check your queue, then press it yourself.

paragraphs.heading: Stop is a request
paragraphs.text: If you do need to stop it, this asks it to stop. A video already going up may still finish.

paragraphs.heading: What went up
paragraphs.text: Afterwards the log lists everything, with its YouTube link, and exports to a spreadsheet.

paragraphs.heading: So, the order
paragraphs.text: Import, queue a few, set visibility to unlisted, then run it once and check the result.
